title: The DynaSim replication scorecard
intro: We ran four blind tests of the Microcosm Dynamics pipeline against published results from the Urban Institute's DYNASIM3. We registered each test in public before its one scored run and scored its output only after we committed it. [src: issue #42 Registrations 13, 15, 16, 17; track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:9,17] In one test, the COLA cut, our benefit changes land within 0.74 points of DYNASIM3's in every age group. The other three each point to a specific place where our pipeline gives a different answer, and every gap is shown below. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:87; fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:163-166; track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:362-366; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:5,118]

cards.title: 1 · COLA cut
cards.policy: Policy: cut each year's cost-of-living adjustment by 1 percentage point from 2010. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:3]
cards.result: Result: in 2030 we are within 0.74 points of DYNASIM3 in all five age groups, and 0.38 points off on average. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:196-199]

cards.title: 2 · 13% cut
cards.policy: Policy: cut all Social Security benefits by 13% from 2004. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:3]
cards.result: Result: adjusted poverty at 67 rises 0.465 points for us and 2 points for DYNASIM3. Only 4 of our 483 people cross the line. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:240,252,494-497]

cards.title: 3 · FRA to 68
cards.policy: Policy: raise the full retirement age gradually to 68. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:3]
cards.result: Result: at ages 65–69, average benefits in 2030 fall 5.68% for us and 9.90% for DYNASIM3, a gap of 4.22 points. The average gap across all five age groups is 1.17. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:569,573,578,687-690]

cards.title: 4 · Minimum benefit
cards.policy: Policy: introduce a minimum Social Security benefit, scored on four versions. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:716,721]
cards.result: Result: under the headline option, 7.75% of beneficiaries aged 62+ receive the minimum for us and 6.3% for DYNASIM3. In our primary specification we are lower for men and higher for women under every option, and three of six registered alternatives break that split. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:732,736; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:118]

method.title: How a blind test works
steps: **Plan.** We write a specification that fixes the statistic, the cells, the one scored row and the registered alternatives, then freeze it. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:13; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:37,43; heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:31] Nothing in it can change after the results come in. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:297]

**Forecast.** Before the run, a forecaster who has not seen DYNASIM3's numbers writes down, with 80% intervals, what our pipeline will produce, what DYNASIM3 printed, and how big the gap will be. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:40-50; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:200-217] The forecast is hashed, so any later edit would show. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:191-196]

**Register on issue #42.** A public comment on issue #42 records the exact code commit, the specification and the forecast before anything runs. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:11-14; fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:68-70]

**One scored run under a supervisor.** Each registration's code runs once, under a process supervisor (launchd), with no retry under that registration. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:15; track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:17; heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:34] If a pre-registered guard stops a run, that refusal is published too. Registration 14 stopped before scoring: its run had tabulated the primary row in memory, but it printed and recorded no value, and the seal stayed closed. Its fix and Registration 15 are public. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:184-187]

**Commit the output, then open the seal.** The output is checked against a list, then committed. Only after that does anyone open the sealed DYNASIM3 numbers. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:16-17; heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:35]

**Publish regardless.** The comparison is posted to #42 whatever it shows. No result is a pass or a fail, because there is no acceptance threshold. [src: heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:36; track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:9]
notes: **What the seal is.** Before the run, DYNASIM3's published numbers are transcribed or digitized, and each file gets a SHA-256 fingerprint. The builders, reviewers and forecaster work blind under a restricted-files list, and each registration discloses its exposures. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:5,22,190] When the seal is opened, a script recomputes every fingerprint and stops before reading any DYNASIM3 value if a file is missing or changed. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:28] The seal shows that the comparator files did not change, and the order of events shows that we committed each output before its seal opened. Neither can show whether anyone saw a published DYNASIM3 value, so a test is blind only as far as each registration's disclosed exposures show. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:188-190; track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:378-381]

**Why the order matters.** Our output is committed before the seal is opened, so it cannot be adjusted after the comparison. Every gap is a result, and none is a target to tune toward. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:9,188]

exercises.title: Exercise 1 · Cut the COLA by 1 percentage point

sections.title: The policy
sections.body: Each year's cost-of-living adjustment is 1 percentage point smaller than under current law, starting in 2010. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:3] In the primary row, the first reduced COLA takes effect in December 2009. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:148]

sections.title: What we measured
sections.body: The percent change in average Social Security benefits in 2030, by the beneficiary's age in 2030. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:44] Our numbers come from the Track A pipeline: a PSID-seeded 2010 cohort, 2008-vintage mortality and disability rates, the 2008 Trustees Report's intermediate COLA and wage-index paths, and the statutory rule that starts COLAs in the year of eligibility. The projections do not check insured status. Benefits come from a transitional Python benefit calculator, averaged over 20 random draws. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:15,19,87-91] DYNASIM3's numbers come from Figure 2 of Urban Institute (2010), *Details Matter* (run 614, 2008 Trustees assumptions). The figure was digitized twice, independently, and the two readings were reconciled. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:5]

sections.title: How to read the chart
sections.body: The green dot is our value. Its bar is our noise: in each cell, the larger of the spread across the 20 draws and the noise floor. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:50-143] The violet mark is DYNASIM3's digitized value. Its bar is the digitization interval, the range the reconciled readings allow for the plotted bar. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:25-31] Values are negative because the policy cuts benefits. A positive gap means our cut is shallower than DYNASIM3's. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:25]

sections.title: What happened
sections.body:
| Age in 2030 | Ours | DYNASIM3 | Gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 50–61 | −7.77 | −7.15 | −0.62 |
| 62–64 | −3.64 | −3.79 | +0.14 |
| 65–69 | −6.26 | −6.36 | +0.10 |
| 70–79 | −12.22 | −11.94 | −0.28 |
| 80+ | −17.92 | −18.66 | +0.74 |

[src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:50-143]

- Across the five cells the average gap is 0.38 points, and the largest is 0.74, at 80+. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:196-199]
- 62–64 and 65–69 fall within our own sampling noise. 50–61, 70–79 and 80+ fall outside it; 80+ is 8.6 times its noise floor. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:31,36-37]
- The five cells rank in the same order as DYNASIM3's. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:38]
- All five of our values fell inside the blind forecast's 80% intervals. Four of the five gaps fell inside the forecast's gap intervals; the 80+ gap (+0.74) lies just past its upper bound of +0.7. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:52-54]

sections.title: Registered alternatives
sections.body:
Each alternative row changes one convention on the same projection. It shows how much the answer depends on choices the published figure doesn't pin down. R0 remains the scored row. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:57-67; scorecard/scorecard-data.json:146-151]

- **R6, the PSID 2009 wave:** average gap 0.37, nearly identical to R0, so the result is not an artifact of the 2011 wave. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:189-193]
- **R4, December 2030 monthly benefit:** 80+ comes within 0.06, but every other cell is 0.8–1.5 points deeper than DYNASIM3. No single registered timing convention matches DYNASIM3 in all five cells. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:181-186; track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:75]
- **R2, entitlement clock:** the worst row, with an average gap of 1.47. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:167-172]

sections.title: Candidate explanations — untested
sections.body:
- **80+ (+0.74), untested.** DYNASIM3's −18.66 lies beyond −18.56, the deepest cut any member of the group can reach under R0's convention. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:74] The memo's untested hypothesis is that DYNASIM3 times the oldest cohorts differently, or that its oldest cell has a different mix, such as survivor benefits on older clocks. The published figure cannot tell these apart. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:76]
- **50–61 (−0.62), untested.** This cell is almost all disabled workers. The hypothesis is that our opening disability stock carries longer durations, or that our 2008-vintage disability rates differ from DYNASIM3's disability model. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:78-79]
- **70–79 (−0.28), untested.** The hypothesis is composition: the share of survivors and converted disabled workers on older clocks. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:81-82]

sections.title: What this does not show
sections.body: It does not show parity with DYNASIM4, a certification, Axiom-computed benefits, or a forward-mode engine projection, which is Track B's job. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:95-99] The exercise is largely mechanical once the COLA clock is fixed, so it tests behaviour only weakly. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:101]

sections.title: The policy
sections.body: Every Social Security benefit is cut by 13%, starting in 2004. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:3]

sections.title: What we measured
sections.body: The change in the adjusted poverty rate at age 67 for people born 1936–45, in percentage points: the poverty rate with the cut minus the rate without it. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:230; track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:36-39] Our numbers are a static calculation on incomes observed in the PSID. It covers people at exact age 67 born in 1937, 1939, 1941, 1943 and 1945, 483 in all, and the cut is applied to their incomes after the fact. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:51,370] DYNASIM3's numbers come from Butrica and Uccello (2004), *How Will Boomers Fare at Retirement?*, Tables 19 and 21. Those tables print only poverty levels, so DYNASIM3's change is Table 21 minus Table 19. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:5]

sections.title: How to read the chart
sections.body: The green dot is our change. Its bar is our design standard error. Divorced and never married have no bar: nobody's poverty status changes in those cells, so their uncertainty cannot be estimated. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:245,385,413; track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:127] The violet mark is DYNASIM3's printed change. Its bar is the ±1-point rounding interval, because both printed levels are whole numbers. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:43-45]

sections.title: What happened
sections.body:
| Group | n | Ours | DYNASIM3 (interval) | Gap |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| All | 483 | 0.465 | 2 (1 to 3) | −1.54 |
| Women | 249 | 0.35 | 3 (2 to 4) | −2.65 |
| Men | 234 | 0.60 | 1 (0 to 2) | −0.40 |
| Married | 331 | 0.60 | 1 (0 to 2) | −0.40 |
| Widowed | 44 | 0.45 | 2 (1 to 3) | −1.55 |
| Divorced | 60 | 0 (no switcher) | 5 (4 to 6) | −5.00 |
| Never married | 14 | 0 (no switcher) | 5 (4 to 6) | −5.00 |

[src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:236-430]

- Our change is smaller than DYNASIM3's in all seven groups. Only men and married fall inside DYNASIM3's rounding interval. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:79-81]
- Our poverty levels are lower too: 3.08% rising to 3.54% for everyone, against DYNASIM3's 5% rising to 7%. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:241-244,253-256]
- The average gap across the seven groups is 2.36 points. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:434-436]
- The headline is coarse. Only 4 of the 483 people cross the poverty line, and one person of average weight moves the headline by 0.207 points. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:111]
- The blind forecast put every DYNASIM3 printed change inside its 80% intervals. It overestimated our own values: it expected 9 switchers and got 4, and our headline of 0.465 fell below its [0.71, 2.32] range. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:259,296-299,305]

sections.title: Registered alternatives
sections.body:
Each alternative row changes one field of the headline row, U0. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:179]

- **U1, all ten birth years** (1936 included, at 68 and uncut), is the closest to DYNASIM3's birth-year mix. It raises the headline to 0.616, still 1.38 below DYNASIM3. No registered row reaches DYNASIM3's 1-to-3 interval. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:237,374]
- **Five rows equal U0 in every cell:** no SSI response, full SSI recomputation, employer DC balances, the SSA 2004 life table and the Census size-by-children matrix. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:468-492] The mechanisms ran, but they moved nobody across the threshold. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:225-233]

sections.title: Candidate explanations — untested
sections.body:
The memo lists these as hypotheses. All are untested, and none will be tuned away. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:309]

- **Lower levels, untested.** The candidates are fewer low-income non-married people in the PSID at 67 (coverage and attrition), counting the whole family unit's income, keeping income sources the report does not name, and differences in how wealth is measured. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:343-349] One fact narrows the search: our lower level is already there in money income, before the annuity and the cut (3.79% for everyone, against DYNASIM3's adjusted 5%). [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:325-330]
- **Smaller change, untested.** The candidates are few people close to the line, self-reported Social Security that may be net of Medicare Part B, and realized 2004–2012 incomes set against a 1992-based projection. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:350-353]

sections.title: What this does not show
sections.body: It is a static simulation on PSID-observed incomes. It is not a projection, and the Dynamics projection engine was not run. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:370] It does not show parity with DYNASIM4, Axiom-computed rules, or a certification. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:371-373] The two largest gaps, divorced and never married, are in cells where nobody crossed the line, so their uncertainty cannot be estimated. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:366,375]

exercises.title: Exercise 3 · Raise the full retirement age to 68

sections.title: The policy
sections.body: The full retirement age rises gradually to 68. The increase starts in 2010 and applies in full to people turning 62 in 2022 or later. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:3]

sections.title: What we measured
sections.body: The same statistic as exercise 1: the percent change in average Social Security benefits in 2030, by age. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:527] Ours comes from exercise 1's projection, path for path, with claim ages held fixed and 20 draws. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:15-18,30] DYNASIM3's comes from the "Increase FRA to 68" bars in the same Urban (2010) Figure 2. They were digitized twice, independently, reconciled, and checked again with a separate pixel-only reading. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:5]

sections.title: How to read the chart
sections.body: The green dot is our value, and its bar is the larger of the draw spread and the noise floor. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:530-620] The violet mark is DYNASIM3's digitized bar, with its sealed interval. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:32-38] At 50–61 the figure draws no bar. DYNASIM3's 0.000 there is a reading, and only the lower end of its interval is a real chart bound. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:58-61]

sections.title: What happened
sections.body:
| Age in 2030 | Ours | DYNASIM3 | Gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 50–61 | −0.003 | 0.000 (reading) | −0.003 |
| 62–64 | −4.73 | −5.12 | +0.39 |
| 65–69 | −5.68 | −9.90 | +4.22 |
| 70–79 | −5.24 | −4.15 | −1.09 |
| 80+ | −0.75 | −0.60 | −0.14 |

[src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:530-620]

- The average gap is 1.17 points. The 65–69 gap of 4.22 accounts for 72% of the summed gaps by itself. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:42]
- DYNASIM3's cut at 65–69 is 1.74 times ours. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:52]
- No cell is within our own noise. 50–61 is consistent with DYNASIM3 at the resolution the chart can show, and 80+ is 0.03 outside its interval. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:43-45,64]
- The middle two cells swap places: DYNASIM3 cuts 62–64 more than 70–79, and we cut 70–79 more than 62–64. Nine of the ten pairs of cells rank in the same order. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:48-51]
- All five of our values fell inside the blind forecast's intervals. Its gap interval missed at 65–69, where the actual gap is 3.31 above its upper bound. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:80-82]

sections.title: Registered alternatives
sections.body:
Every registered row has its largest gap at 65–69, and none comes within 3.9 points of DYNASIM3 there. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:110]

- **F3, people claiming at 65 or later delay by the increase:** 65–69 moves further away, to a gap of 5.66, because postponed claimants leave the set of people receiving benefits under the reform. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:645-650]
- **F5, mean of individual ratios:** the lowest average gap, 1.08, and still 3.96 at its worst cell. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:659-664]
- **The union-ratio diagnostic** averages over everyone alive in the age group. For F3 it gives −8.68 at 65–69. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:135-137] That is observed arithmetic, and it is not a diagnosis. It is not a registered row, it is not scored, and it cannot be promoted; it is a question for a future registration. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:138]

sections.title: Candidate explanations — untested
sections.body:
All are untested, and none will be tuned away. Run 614's claiming, earnings-test treatment and phase-in were not verified. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:117]

- **What we do know about 65–69.** Everyone in the cell was born 1961–65 and faces a 12-month increase. At fixed claim ages, that cuts a retired worker's benefit by 6.25% to 7.69%, depending on claim age; a spouse's excess falls by at most 10.00%; a disabled worker's benefit does not change. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:121-125] No mix of these reaches −9.90, short of a cell made almost entirely of spouses' excesses starting at 65. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:126]
- **(a) The earnings test extended to 68, untested.** Our model holds the earnings test's parameters but applies no earnings test, and it pays gross amounts. Testing this idea needs forward earnings in the projection, which Track B plans to add. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:128-131]
- **(b) A claiming response averaged over everyone in the age group, untested.** If DYNASIM3's average runs over everyone in the age group, a postponed claimant counts as zero under the reform. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:132-134]
- **70–79, untested.** The phase-in schedule and a claiming response at the retirement age both point the right way. Neither is tested. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:146-148]
- **62–64, untested.** The candidate is composition: disabled workers hold 26.7% of our baseline dollars in this cell, and their benefits don't change. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:151-152]

sections.title: What this does not show
sections.body: It does not show parity with DYNASIM4, a certification, or Axiom-computed benefits. Forward-mode projection, behavioral claiming and forward earnings belong to Track B. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:171-174] It tests the parts Track A leaves out sharply and the mechanical part it models only weakly. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:169] It does not tell us DYNASIM3's mechanism at 65–69. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:117,126-127]

exercises.title: Exercise 4 · Introduce a minimum Social Security benefit

sections.title: The policy
sections.body: A minimum benefit puts a floor under the benefit formula's result, the PIA. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:56; scorecard/scorecard-data.json:1056-1058] The 2006 report's Table 6 shows several versions. This exercise scores four: option 2 (standard, price-indexed), option 3 (standard, wage-indexed), option 4 (generous, price-indexed) and option 5 (generous, wage-indexed). [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:86-91]

sections.title: What we measured
sections.body: The share of OASDI beneficiaries aged 62 and older who receive the minimum, for everyone, men and women, under each option. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:721] Someone counts if they are paid a worker's benefit that rests on a minimum PIA, or a linked spouse's or survivor's benefit that rests on one. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:56] Ours is a static measurement on 2,135 PSID beneficiaries in income year 2022. DYNASIM3's is a 2025 projection from Favreault, Mermin and Steuerle (2006), Table 6 (run 432). [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:54,66-68,76; scorecard/scorecard-data.json:725]

sections.title: How to read the chart
sections.body: The green dot is our share. Its bar is the larger of our design SE and our noise floor. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:103; scorecard/scorecard-data.json:726-1038] The violet mark is DYNASIM3's printed share. The report prints one decimal place, so its rounding interval is only ±0.05 points and barely shows. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:97]

sections.title: What happened
sections.body:
| Option · group | Ours | DYNASIM3 | Gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 · All (headline) | 7.75 | 6.3 | +1.45 |
| 2 · Men | 2.36 | 4.8 | −2.44 |
| 2 · Women | 11.67 | 7.6 | +4.07 |
| 3 · All | 11.12 | 11.3 | −0.18 |

sections.title: Registered alternatives
sections.body:
Each alternative changes one registered field, and none is promoted to the scored row. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:139]

- **MS5, benefit-implied PIA,** comes closest, with an average gap of 1.60 against the headline's 4.09. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:1042-1045,1080-1086] It raises men's shares under every option and lowers women's under every option. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:252] That is observed arithmetic, and it is not a diagnosis: the contrast does not identify what causes the gap against DYNASIM3. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:270] Its lower gap gives no authority to replace MS0. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:150]
- **MS1, the report's own 2007 policy year,** moves the headline to 6.83. That shows our window rule matters; it does not show how DYNASIM3 dated the policy. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:143,273]

sections.title: Candidate explanations — untested
sections.body:
Each is untested, and none was tuned. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:270]

- **Vintage, untested:** realized 2022 PSID outcomes are compared with a 2025 projection. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:272]
- **PIA source and earnings histories, untested:** where both measures exist, the benefit-implied PIA is a median 1.11 times the history-based one, with wide spread. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:275]
- **Disability origin, untested:** 407 of the records in the policy window started as disability benefits. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:276]
- **Unlinked auxiliaries, untested:** 60 spouses or survivors we cannot link to a worker count as not receiving. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:277]
- **Exposure and age structure, and wage and price paths, untested.** [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:273-274]

sections.title: What this does not show
sections.body: It is a static measurement on realized PSID outcomes for income year 2022, using Python rules. It is not a projection, and it does not test the Dynamics projection engine. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:295] The comparator is DYNASIM3, not DYNASIM4. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:295] PSID does not observe Social Security coverage, so all PSID labor income counts as covered earnings, including earnings that are not covered. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:297]

reading.title: Reading the numbers
reading.body:
- **Gap.** Our value minus DYNASIM3's, in the exercise's units. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:25] A gap is a disagreement between two models, not an error in either. In exercises 1 and 3, both numbers project 2030 effects of reforms that were never enacted, so no one can observe the true effect. In exercises 2 and 4, ours apply the policy statically to incomes already observed in the PSID, with no projection, and DYNASIM3's are projections published in 2004 and 2006. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:3; fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:3; track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:32,353,370; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:272,295] When a policy cuts benefits, a positive gap means our cut is shallower. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:119]
- **Mean absolute gap.** The average size of the gaps across an exercise's scored cells, ignoring sign: 5 cells in exercises 1 and 3, 7 in exercise 2 and 12 in exercise 4. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:35; track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:171; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:5]
- **Noise floor (the half-sample split).** We split the sample into two halves with no person or family unit in both, compute the statistic on each half, and average how far apart the halves land over five random splits. That measures how much our number moves on sampling alone. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:33; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:60] It is measured at half-sample size and not rescaled, so it overstates the noise in the full sample. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:42,97]
- **Design SE.** A standard error that accounts for how the PSID sample was drawn (its strata and clusters). [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:41; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:60]
- **Rounding interval.** A printed table rounds its numbers, so the true value lies within half a unit of the last printed digit: ±0.05 for exercise 4's one-decimal shares, and ±1 for exercise 2's change between two whole-number levels. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:97; track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:43-45] It describes DYNASIM3's printing; it is not a confidence interval. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:62]
- **Digitization interval.** When DYNASIM3's number is a bar on a chart, the interval is the range the reconciled readings of that bar allow. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:5,25]
- **Static vs projection.** Exercises 1 and 3 project a PSID-seeded 2010 cohort to 2030 along fixed paths. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:19,87-91] Exercises 2 and 4 apply the policy to incomes already observed in the PSID, with no projection. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:370; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:295]
- **Registered alternative row.** A variant, fixed before the run, that changes one field of the headline row. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:139] A smaller gap in an alternative shows that the result is sensitive to how it is implemented; it does not reveal DYNASIM3's mechanism, and no alternative is ever promoted. [src: microcosm-dynamics docs/design/urban2010_track_a_v2.md:931; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:139]
- **One-shot.** Each registration gets one run, and its scored output is the result. There is no acceptance threshold, and the result is reported rather than graded pass or fail. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:9]
- **Post hoc.** A rerun designed after seeing a result. We label such a rerun "registered, one-shot, post hoc, not blind" and report it beside the original, which it never replaces. Track A v2, the planned post hoc rerun of exercises 1 and 3, has no registration yet, and so far we have tested its code only on invented data. [src: microcosm-dynamics docs/design/urban2010_track_a_v2.md:7,34,41]

sections.title: Scope
sections.body: The four blind tests exercise only part of the model. Exercises 1 and 3 follow a PSID cohort forward from 2010 and draw no earnings after 2010. Exercises 2 and 4 apply the policy to incomes the PSID already recorded, with no projection. [src: microcosm-dynamics src/populace_dynamics/cola_track_a/adapters.py:25-27,140-146; track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:370; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:295] In the table, "Planned" marks work a written plan covers, and a dash marks a component with no documented next step.

sections.title: Don't you have longitudinal earnings?
sections.body:
Yes. The PSID records head and spouse labor income for income years 1968–2022: every year through 1996, then every two years. [src: microcosm-dynamics src/populace_dynamics/data/family.py:10,25-27,52-55] We impute the years the panel does not report or set them to zero, and those years make up about half of the career years behind exercises 1 and 3. [src: track-c-aime-agreement-20260924-master/RESULTS.md:100-106] Exercises 1 and 3 read these careers through 2010, and exercise 4 reads a longer span, adding later odd years from the next wave's reports. We treat all labor income as covered earnings. [src: microcosm-dynamics src/populace_dynamics/cohorts/psid2010.py:51-57; microcosm-dynamics src/populace_dynamics/min_benefit_track_m/careers.py:7-16,10] Gate 1 scores a generated backcast earnings process against held-out panel moments. It does not certify the recorded careers the tests read. [src: microcosm-dynamics gates.yaml:120-124]

We also fit a forward earnings law for ages 25–64. It draws new earnings every second year and carries them forward in between. [src: microcosm-dynamics src/populace_dynamics/engine/forward_earnings.py:1-13,64-67,1030-1031] It passed gate_m6, a temporal holdout, on 4 of 5 seeds. Its parameters use only data through 2014, but we selected its structure with the later waves in view, and gate_m6 does not certify that selection. [src: microcosm-dynamics gates.yaml gate_m6.not_certified spec_selection_in_sample, forward_earnings_law_not_gate1_certified] gate_m6 scores earnings cells for 2016 and 2018 and flows for 2015–2019, and treats the 2020–2022 window as diagnostic only. It certifies nothing about mortality drift. [src: microcosm-dynamics runs/gate_m6_candidate3_v1.json:2-7,33; microcosm-dynamics gates.yaml:5381,5394-5415,5447]

The four blind tests don't draw forward earnings yet. Track A, which runs exercises 1 and 3, opens in 2010 and draws no earnings after that year. [src: microcosm-dynamics src/populace_dynamics/cola_track_a/adapters.py:140-146,238] The code states the reason: we fit the forward law from a 2014 boundary, four years after Track A's opening. [src: microcosm-dynamics src/populace_dynamics/cola_track_a/adapters.py:25-27] The law has no fitted distribution above 64 and draws older people's earnings from its oldest age band. The engine assigns a fixed zero to anyone without a fitted 2014 earnings state. [src: microcosm-dynamics src/populace_dynamics/engine/forward_earnings.py:218-222; src/populace_dynamics/engine/earnings_domain.py:1-6] Exercises 2 and 4 are static, so they need no forward earnings. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:370; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:295]

We plan to wire forward earnings in through Track B. We would carry a 2010 cohort's earnings state forward to 2014, add a history recorder for 2010–2030 and fit a forward law for ages 25–69. [src: trackb-design-20260928.md:121,125,127] We have built none of it yet.

next.title: What comes next
next.body:
**Track B.** Track B is planned work in three parts: forward earnings to 2030, the retirement earnings test and a claiming hazard to replace the fixed claim-age distribution. Each mechanism is admitted separately, and only through a registered gate against independent observations. [src: trackb-design-20260928.md:15] The aim is to make two things testable: the projected-population targets, and exercise 3's earnings-test hypothesis. [src: trackb-design-20260928.md:17-19] No DYNASIM comparison may select its structure, parameters or rows, and agreement with DYNASIM never rescues a failed gate. [src: trackb-design-20260928.md:21] The plan does not yet deliver validated 2030 earnings, validated ages 65–69, earnings-test effects on any population, validated monthly timing, or any explanation of exercise 3's 65–69 gap. [src: trackb-design-20260928.md:264-269]

**The next held-out target.** The next target is the 1946–55 birth-cohort column of the same Boomers 2004 tables. It is scored on exercise 2's cells: the change in adjusted poverty at 67 under a uniform 13% cut. [src: heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:7] A validation lane will confirm the column and cells without showing the builders any value, and will publish a definition-only statement with no values or directions. [src: heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:14,40] Exercise 2 came out below DYNASIM3 on both level and change. A second cohort tests whether that pattern follows the income concept or the cohort, though it will not say which mechanism is responsible. [src: heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:15] Like exercise 2, it does not test the projection engine. [src: heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:19] A conditional second target, a third policy option from the same Urban (2010) figure, proceeds only after a validation lane clears its formula. [src: heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:9]

**Track A v2 (post hoc).** Track A v2 would rerun exercises 1 and 3 together. It would add the statutory disability computation years, chosen because the statute requires them rather than to close a gap, and, as a separate mechanism, dual entitlement to disability and spouse's benefits. [src: microcosm-dynamics docs/design/urban2010_track_a_v2.md:1,8,26-28] Its code is in the repository, so far we have tested it only on invented data, and it has no registration yet. Its design labels it "registered, one-shot, post hoc, not blind", and we would report it beside v1, where it would never replace a v1 row. [src: microcosm-dynamics docs/design/urban2010_track_a_v2.md:34,41] A smaller gap there would show that the result is sensitive to implementation; it would not show DYNASIM3's mechanism. [src: microcosm-dynamics docs/design/urban2010_track_a_v2.md:931]

drill.question: What is DYNASIM3, and what are we claiming about it?
drill.answer: It is the Urban Institute's historical dynamic microsimulation model. We present each test as an open, checkable comparison with its published numbers, and we claim neither parity with DYNASIM4 nor that our pipeline replaces it. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:5,95-99] *(exercise 1 memo)*

drill.question: What does "one-shot" mean?
drill.answer: Each registration gets one run, and its scored output is the result, whatever it shows. There is no acceptance threshold, so nothing passes or fails. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:9] *(exercise 1 memo)*

drill.question: Which exercise matches, and how closely?
drill.answer: Exercise 1, the COLA cut: within 0.74 points in every age group and 0.38 on average, with the five cells in DYNASIM3's order. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:35,38] *(exercise 1 memo)*

drill.question: What is the seal, and why is it opened after the commit?
drill.answer: It holds SHA-256 fingerprints of DYNASIM3's transcribed numbers, and a script checks them before reading any value. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:28] Opening it only after our output is committed means the output cannot be changed after the comparison. Neither the seal nor the order of events can show whether anyone saw a published DYNASIM3 value, so a test is blind only as far as each registration's disclosed exposures show. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:188-189] *(exercise 2 and 3 memos)*

drill.question: Why is exercise 1 a weak test of behaviour?
drill.answer: Once the COLA clock is fixed, the exercise is largely mechanical. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:101] *(exercise 1 memo)*

drill.question: What is the difference between the noise floor and the rounding interval?
drill.answer: The noise floor measures our own sampling noise: how far two person-disjoint half samples land from each other. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:33] The rounding interval measures how far DYNASIM3's unrounded number could be from what the report printed. Neither one is a confidence interval. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:62,97] *(exercise 1 and 4 memos)*

drill.question: Why are 4 switchers a problem in exercise 2?
drill.answer: The headline change rests on 4 people out of 483 crossing the poverty line, and one person of average weight moves it by 0.207 points. So the estimate is coarse. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:111,375] *(exercise 2 memo)*

drill.question: Why do five exercise 2 alternatives give exactly the headline?
drill.answer: The SSI, retirement-account, life-table and threshold mechanisms all ran, but none moved anyone across the poverty line. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:225-233] *(exercise 2 memo)*

drill.question: Why does exercise 4 compare 2022 to 2025?
drill.answer: Ours is a static measurement on the PSID's 2023 wave, which reports income year 2022. DYNASIM3's figure is a projection for 2025. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:54; scorecard/scorecard-data.json:725] The vintage difference is a candidate explanation for the gaps, and it is untested. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:272] *(exercise 4 memo)*

drill.question: Option 3, All, is within 0.18 points. Why isn't that a match?
drill.answer: Because the near-agreement hides opposite gaps: men are 5.47 below and women 3.46 above. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:109-110,118] *(exercise 4 memo)*

drill.question: Why is MS5 not promoted, when its gap is lowest?
drill.answer: MS0 was registered as the only scored row, and the rules forbid choosing a different headline after seeing results. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:43,297] MS5's smaller gap is observed arithmetic, and it is not a diagnosis of why we differ. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:150,270] *(exercise 4 memo)*

drill.question: Why can't fixed claim ages reach −9.9 at 65–69?
drill.answer: Everyone in the cell faces a 12-month increase. At fixed claim ages that cuts a retired worker by 6.25% to 7.69%, a spouse's excess by at most 10%, and a disabled worker not at all. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:121-125] No mix reaches −9.90, short of a cell made almost entirely of spouses' excesses starting at 65, so DYNASIM3's bar carries something beyond the age-factor cut. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:126-127] *(exercise 3 memo)*

drill.question: So is the earnings test the answer at 65–69?
drill.answer: It is a candidate, and it is untested. Our model holds the earnings test's parameters but applies no earnings test, and testing the idea needs forward earnings in the projection, which Track B plans to add. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:128-131] Track B's plan does not yet deliver any explanation of the 65–69 gap. [src: trackb-design-20260928.md:269] *(exercise 3 memo; Track B design §4)*

drill.question: In exercise 1, why does 80+ differ by 0.74 when R4 comes within 0.06?
drill.answer: Under R0's timing, no one aged 80+ can reach DYNASIM3's −18.66; the deepest possible cut is −18.56. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:74] R4 comes within 0.06 at 80+ but is 0.8–1.5 points deeper than DYNASIM3 in every other cell, so no single registered timing convention matches all five. Why DYNASIM3 differs is untested. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:75-76; scorecard/scorecard-data.json:181-186] *(exercise 1 memo)*

tour.title: Four results
tour.body: These are the four tests at a glance: one close result and three specific differences. Each card gives the headline number, not a score. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:87; fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:163-166; track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:362-366; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:5,118]

tour.title: How a blind test works
tour.body: Plan, forecast, register, make one scored run, commit, then open the seal. The timelines show the minutes between those steps. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:201-218]

tour.title: The COLA cut comes close
tour.body: Every age group is within 0.74 points, and 62–64 and 65–69 fall within our own noise. A COLA cut acts mechanically on benefits in payment, so this is a weak test of the model's dynamics. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:35-36]

tour.title: A smaller poverty response
tour.body: Poverty at 67 rises 0.465 points for us and 2 for DYNASIM3. Note how few people cross the line. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:240,252,494-497]

tour.title: The 65–69 gap
tour.body: DYNASIM3's cut at 65–69 is 1.74 times ours, and deeper than fixed claim ages can produce. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:52,126]

tour.title: Split by sex
tour.body: The options rank the same way, but we are lower for men and higher for women every time. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:5,118]

tour.title: Reading the numbers
tour.body: Our noise and DYNASIM3's rounding are different things, and the charts show both. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:62]

tour.title: What comes next
tour.body: Track B would make the earnings-test hypothesis at 65–69 testable. A new held-out target already sits under the seal, and a planned post hoc rerun would sit beside v1. [src: trackb-design-20260928.md:17-19; heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:7; microcosm-dynamics docs/design/urban2010_track_a_v2.md:41]

presenter.title: 60 seconds
presenter.body: We ran four blind tests against the Urban Institute's DYNASIM3. [src: issue #42 Registrations 13, 15, 16, 17] We registered each one in public, gave it one scored run, and compared it only after we'd committed the output. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:9,17] The COLA cut comes close: every age group is within 0.74 points, 0.38 on average, though a COLA cut acts mechanically on benefits in payment. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:35] Raising the full retirement age to 68, we differ from DYNASIM3 by 4.2 points at 65 to 69, where DYNASIM3's cut is deeper than fixed claim ages can produce in our pipeline. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:117,126-127] A 13% cut raises poverty at 67 by 0.465 points for us and 2 for DYNASIM3, and only 4 of our 483 people cross the line. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:240,252,494-497] On a minimum benefit we're at 7.75% against 6.3%, in our primary specification lower for men and higher for women under every option. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:732,736; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:118] Every explanation is untested, and every gap stays on the page. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:270] Next, Track B plans to bring forward earnings into the projections, apply the earnings test and add a claiming hazard, so the earnings-test hypothesis at 65–69 becomes testable. [src: trackb-design-20260928.md:15-19]

presenter.title: 3 minutes
presenter.body:
DYNASIM3 is the Urban Institute's historical dynamic microsimulation model. We set out to reproduce four of its published Social Security results in a way anyone can check. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:5,95-99]

The method comes first, because it's what makes the numbers mean anything. For each exercise we froze a specification and had a forecaster who hadn't seen DYNASIM3's numbers predict our result, theirs and the gap. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:13; track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:40] We posted the registration on issue #42, made one scored run, and committed the output. Only then did we open the sealed file of DYNASIM3's numbers. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:11-17] We had no pass mark, and we publish either way. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:9]

Exercise 1 cuts the COLA by a point. We're within 0.74 points of DYNASIM3 in all five age groups, and all five cells rank in the same order. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:35,38] That test is largely mechanical, so it is a weak test of behavioral dynamics. [src: track-a-oneshot-20260923/COMPARISON.md:101]

Exercise 3 raises the full retirement age to 68. We're close at the youngest and oldest ages, but at 65 to 69 DYNASIM3 cuts benefits by 9.9% and we cut them by 5.7%. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:34-38] With claim ages held fixed, a retired worker in that cell loses at most 7.69%, so DYNASIM3's bar carries something beyond the age-factor cut at fixed claim ages. We don't know what. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:124-127] The candidates are an earnings test extended to 68 and a claiming response averaged over everyone in the age group. Both are untested. [src: fra68-oneshot-reg15-20260925/COMPARISON.md:128-134]

Exercise 2 cuts every benefit by 13%. Poverty at 67 rises 0.465 points for us and 2 for DYNASIM3, and our poverty levels are lower to begin with. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:362-364] Only 4 of our 483 people cross the line, so our estimate is coarse. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:111]

Exercise 4 adds a minimum benefit. Under the headline option we put 7.75% of beneficiaries on the minimum, against DYNASIM3's 6.3%. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:732,736] The options rank the same way, but in our primary specification we're lower for men and higher for women under every option, and three of six registered alternatives break that split. [src: track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:5,118] One registered alternative, which builds the PIA from the benefit people actually receive, cuts the average gap from 4.09 to 1.60. We don't promote it: that's arithmetic we observed, and it doesn't diagnose anything. [src: scorecard/scorecard-data.json:1042-1045,1080-1086; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:150,270]

Two of these are static calculations on survey data, and none uses the rules engine. None is a certification or DYNASIM4 parity. [src: track-u-oneshot-reg16-20260927/COMPARISON.md:370-372; track-m-oneshot-reg17-20260927/COMPARISON.md:295]

What's next: Track B plans to bring forward earnings into the projections, apply the earnings test and add a claiming hazard, each behind its own gate, so we can test the earnings-test hypothesis at 65–69 at all. [src: trackb-design-20260928.md:15-19] A new held-out target, the next birth cohort in the poverty tables, is already under the exercise-2 seal, and its builders will work without seeing any of its values. [src: heldout-target-pick-20260928.md:7,14] A post hoc rerun of exercises 1 and 3 will sit beside the originals and never replace them. [src: microcosm-dynamics docs/design/urban2010_track_a_v2.md:1,41]
